subject: International Relations
title: South Asia, Afghanistan, and Nuclear and Contemporary Security

segments.text: For South Asian and Afghanistan topics, use a consistent causal sequence: background, then the interests of the major actors involved, then the immediate trigger or negotiation process, then external involvement, then consequences, then the obstacles still standing in the way of settlement — keep legal, territorial, security, economic, and domestic-political dimensions separate before bringing them together in a final evaluation. For nuclear and other emerging-domain issues, identify the capability or threat, the strategic mechanism at work, the response it may provoke from others, and the resulting effect on stability — never assume that greater capability automatically produces greater security.

blocks.text: A. India-Pakistan Relations and Territorial Disputes

segments.text: Peace-making seeks an agreement to stop or manage conflict; peace-building addresses the deeper institutions, relationships, and causes actually needed for durable peace — South Asian disputes involve security dilemmas, borders, identity, water, allegations of terrorism, domestic politics, and great-power influence together, and confidence-building measures can meaningfully lower risk even where final settlements remain absent. India and Pakistan have used wars, bilateral agreements, back-channel contacts, and formal dialogue together to manage a deeply conflictual relationship; important reference points include the Indus Waters Treaty, the Simla Agreement, the Lahore process, various ceasefire arrangements, and the Composite Dialogue framework — exact legal claims about any of these should always come from the actual treaty texts rather than secondhand political summaries.
The 1960
Indus Waters Treaty

, brokered with World Bank involvement, allocates use of the eastern and western river systems through detailed rules, and creates the Permanent Indus Commission plus dispute-resolution mechanisms; water disputes under it typically involve interpretation of specific project design and treaty procedures, rather than a simple claim that one side “owns all the water.”
Sir Creek
is a maritime-boundary-linked dispute in the Rann of Kutch area;
Siachen

concerns military positions around the glacier region and differing interpretations of the line beyond map coordinate NJ9842 — both cases show how unresolved mapping and ongoing security concerns can create real strategic costs even in remote, sparsely populated areas. Societal links — visas, people-to-people contacts, trade, and civil-society engagement — can reduce mutual stereotypes, build constituencies genuinely invested in peace, and create economic interests in stability; however, security crises can quickly restrict visas, transport, and trade, and civil-society engagement cannot substitute for actual state negotiation on the core disputes, even though it can help sustain communication between the two sides in the meantime.

blocks.text: B. Afghanistan from the Cold War to the Present

segments.text: Afghanistan became a major Cold War conflict theatre after the 1979 Soviet intervention, with Afghan resistance receiving substantial external support and Pakistan becoming a genuine frontline state; the war militarized the region, created large refugee flows, and strengthened armed networks whose later trajectories would go on to affect regional security for decades. The 1988
Geneva Accords

created a framework connected with Soviet withdrawal, but did not create a comprehensive internal political settlement among Afghan factions themselves; after the Soviet withdrawal and the subsequent collapse of the Afghan government, civil war among Afghan factions paved the way for the Taliban’s rise during the 1990s — the accords should never be described as having ended Afghanistan’s civil war, since they plainly did not.

The Taliban captured most of Afghanistan during the 1990s and hosted al-Qaeda’s leadership; after the September 11, 2001 attacks, a US-led intervention removed the Taliban government from Kabul and targeted al-Qaeda and Taliban forces directly, with the conflict subsequently evolving into a long insurgency, an international state-building effort, and an extended international military mission. The 2001
Bonn Agreement

established an interim political process that led to new Afghan institutions and a constitution, while international forces and aid supported the post-Taliban state for two decades; the US and allied military withdrawal in 2021 was then followed by the Taliban’s rapid return to national power — this final chapter extends beyond the syllabus’s original wording but is essential for any genuinely current answer on Afghanistan.

blocks.text: C. Nuclear Proliferation, Deterrence, and Arms Control

segments.text: Nuclear proliferation means the spread of nuclear weapons, weapon capabilities, or relevant technologies and materials to additional actors; horizontal proliferation refers to more states acquiring nuclear weapons, while vertical proliferation refers to the expansion or improvement of arsenals already possessed by existing nuclear states — drivers of proliferation include security concerns, prestige, domestic politics, and available technology. India and Pakistan developed their nuclear forces under intense bilateral security competition, producing doctrines and postures focused specifically on deterrence and crisis stability; terms such as credible minimum deterrence, no-first-use debates, full-spectrum deterrence, and tactical nuclear systems should always be drawn from official, authoritative doctrinal sources, since positions on these matters evolve and remain genuinely politically contested.

The nuclear non-proliferation regime combines the NPT (recognizing five nuclear-weapon states under its treaty definition, and resting on non-proliferation, peaceful-use, and disarmament commitments together), IAEA safeguards (which verify compliance), export-control arrangements such as the NSG (an export-control group, not itself a treaty organization), and test-ban efforts, together with broader international norms against proliferation. The 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty (PTBT) prohibits nuclear tests in the atmosphere, outer space, and underwater, though notably not underground; the CTBT seeks to ban all nuclear explosions but has not entered into force, because specified required ratifications remain outstanding; the FMCT refers to proposed negotiations to prohibit production of fissile material for nuclear weapons, but no such treaty is currently in force — the precise status of each of these instruments should be stated carefully rather than assumed to be fully in force universally. Civil nuclear technology can support electricity generation, medicine, agriculture, and research, but sensitive fuel-cycle capabilities create genuine proliferation concerns of their own, which is exactly why international cooperation relies on safeguards, export controls, security standards, and formal agreements to separate peaceful use from weapons risk in practice.

blocks.text: D. Missile Defence, Space, and Great-Power Competition

segments.text: Missile-defence systems aim to detect and intercept incoming missiles; they can genuinely protect against limited attacks, but opponents may respond with more missiles, decoys, or new delivery systems entirely, creating a fresh arms-race dynamic — the actual effect of any missile-defence deployment depends heavily on its technical effectiveness and the wider strategic context it sits within, both among major powers and specifically in South Asia. Militarization of space means using space systems for military support, such as communications, navigation, and intelligence-gathering; weaponization more narrowly refers to actually placing or using weapons for combat in or against space systems themselves — modern militaries depend heavily on satellites, making space infrastructure both strategically important and genuinely vulnerable, and anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons tests specifically create dangerous orbital debris alongside broader escalation risks.

Global strategy increasingly links Euro-Atlantic security with Asia-Pacific and Indo-Pacific competition: US alliances, NATO security commitments, Russia-West confrontation, China’s rise, the Taiwan question, maritime disputes, economic security, and global supply chains all connect these two theatres together in practice, even though “Asia-Pacific” and “Indo-Pacific” reflect partly different strategic framings of the same broad region. A strong answer on this theme prepares the distinct interests of the US, China, Russia, the EU/NATO, and relevant regional powers together, then updates current alignments close to whenever the exam is actually being taken.

Kashmir is a long-running territorial and political dispute rooted in the 1947 partition and accession conflict, followed by subsequent India-Pakistan wars, UN involvement, and competing claims that persist to the present. A sound answer distinguishes the Line of Control clearly from a recognized international boundary, covers the relevant bilateral agreements and UN history accurately, and recognizes the genuine human and political dimensions affecting the Kashmiri population themselves — any resolutions or agreements referenced should be drawn from primary legal or diplomatic documents, never invented quotations or oversimplified claims about legal status.

The Palestine question combines competing national movements, contested territory, occupation, refugees, settlements, security concerns, statehood, and the status of Jerusalem, within roughly a century of continuous conflict. Key reference points include the British Mandate period, the 1947 UN partition recommendation, the 1948 war and resulting refugee crisis, the 1967 occupation, the Oslo process, several subsequent wars, and the continuing debate over a two-state solution or other possible political arrangements — historical facts, legal claims, and political positions should always be kept clearly separate from one another, drawing on UN documents and current humanitarian and diplomatic reporting rather than any single side’s framing alone.

South Asia, Afghanistan, and Nuclear/Contemporary Security key takeaways: India-Pakistan disputes span water, territory, and security together, and each requires its own specific legal and historical grounding rather than a single generic narrative. Afghanistan’s trajectory — Soviet invasion, civil war, Taliban rise, post-9/11 intervention, and 2021 withdrawal — is one connected causal chain, not a series of unrelated episodes. Nuclear proliferation, deterrence, and the non-proliferation regime address genuinely different (though related) problems, and each instrument within that regime (NPT, IAEA, NSG, PTBT, CTBT, FMCT) has its own distinct, precise legal status that should never be assumed to be more settled than it actually is. Missile defence and space weaponization both illustrate how a defensive-seeming capability can still provoke an offsetting reaction from an adversary. Kashmir and Palestine are both genuinely long-running disputes best understood through careful, chronological, and legally precise analysis — not through slogans from any single side of either conflict.

With this, International Relations (Part V) is now complete across both papers: theory and approaches, security and strategy, international political economy and institutions, twentieth-century history, regional organizations and major-power foreign policies, and South Asia and contemporary security. All five subjects — Accountancy & Auditing, Economics, Computer Science, Political Science, and International Relations — are now fully expanded.

Use IR theory as a genuine lens, not decoration: for any event or policy, ask what a realist, a liberal, and a constructivist would each emphasize, and let that comparison drive the analysis. For security and strategy topics, connect the concept to an actor’s actual capability, intention, and the resulting interaction with other actors. For any specific conflict or foreign-policy issue, separate the historical chronology from the ongoing analytical debate about how to interpret it.
